mainTopic: Rentals with payment for damage, and protecting and investing orphans' money without רבית
overview: This amud opens by finishing a discussion about rentals where the renter pays rent and also pays for damage. The גמרא explains that this sailors' custom is valid because a ברייתא permits it. Next, רב ענן quotes שמואל as allowing orphans' money to be lent with רבית. רב נחמן strongly objects and asks for the real story. That story is שמואל renting out the kettle of מר עוקבא's orphans, and רב נחמן shows it was a rental allowed even for adults. A different ruling then allows orphans' money to be invested on terms close to profit and far from loss. A ברייתא adds that for ordinary people such a deal is wicked. Finally, רבה, רב יוסף and רב אשי debate how a בית דין should manage orphans' money. רב אשי's method is to give it, in front of a בית דין, to a trustworthy man with secure property who obeys the court.

steps.title: Sailors pay rent and also pay for breakage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reports a custom: renters pay rent from the moment they take the item and pay for damage if it breaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the sailors are used to paying rent from the time they pull the boat away, and paying for damage if it breaks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real-life custom that matches the arrangement it was just discussing: the renter pays rent and also takes responsibility for damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, if someone pays rent, the owner carries the risk of damage. Here the renter pays both, and the גמרא points out that this is how people actually do business. This sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'men of pitch'; sailors or boatmen
Pulling, taking the item into one's possession

phrases.english: And the sailors are accustomed
to pay rent at the time of pulling,
and to pay for damage at the time of breakage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion on the daf about renting with both rent and responsibility for damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The accepted practice among sailors is to pay rent and also pay for damage.

steps.title: Does the law depend on custom?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a question of רבית can really be decided by what people usually do.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say the matter depends on custom?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last step: how can custom decide whether something is allowed or forbidden?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבית is a Torah prohibition. A custom alone cannot make something forbidden become allowed. So citing what sailors do seems to prove nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (a challenging question)

phrases.english: Is that to say that on custom
the matter depends?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the custom in step 1 can be used as a source.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using the sailors' custom as a basis for permitting the arrangement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Torah prohibition like רבית cannot be decided by custom.

steps.title: The custom is valid because a ברייתא permits it
steps.stepSummary: The custom counts only because a ברייתא already taught that this arrangement is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the ברייתא taught this, it is a proper custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the custom is not the source of the law; the ברייתא is, and the custom simply follows it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling comes from a ברייתא that allows this kind of rental. Since the ברייתא allows it, the sailors' practice is a legitimate custom that people may rely on.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא, a teaching of the תנאים outside the משנה

steps.whatToRemember: Custom is only relied on here because a ברייתא already permits the arrangement.

phrases.english: Because the ברייתא taught it,
it is a custom.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Grounds the custom in an earlier source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The custom alone was being used to permit the arrangement.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא permits it, and the custom follows that ruling.

steps.title: שמואל: orphans' money may be lent with interest
steps.stepSummary: רב ענן reports in the name of שמואל that orphans' money may be lent with רבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ענן said in the name of שמואל: It is permitted to lend orphans' money with interest.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב ענן quotes שמואל as allowing orphans' money to be lent with רבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The orphans are young children who are not yet obligated in מצוות. So it might seem the רבית prohibition does not apply to money taken for them.

keyTerms.meaning: Interest on a loan, forbidden by the Torah

phrases.english: Rav Anan says that Shmuel says:
Money belonging to orphans,
it is permitted to lend it with interest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about רבית and orphans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Orphans' money may be lent with interest (as reported by רב ענן).

steps.title: רב נחמן objects strongly
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן argues that being orphans does not allow us to feed them forbidden money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: Because they are orphans, we feed them forbidden things? Orphans who eat what is not theirs will follow their parents to the grave!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן attacks the statement: we cannot give orphans forbidden gain just because they are orphans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if children are not obligated, adults may not give them forbidden things. Money from רבית is not truly theirs, and רב נחמן warns harshly that this brings punishment on them.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who left them behind, their dead parents

phrases.english: Rav Nahman said to him:
Because they are orphans,
we feed them forbidden things?!
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, but the corrected wording is the word in square brackets, which reads 'we feed'.

phrases.english: Orphans who eat what is not theirs
should go after those who left them!
phrases.notes: A sharp curse: they should follow their dead parents to the grave.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן מִשּׁוּם דְּיַתְמֵי נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly attacks the ruling of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that orphans' money may be lent with רבית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being minors does not let others feed them forbidden gain; money from רבית is not rightfully theirs.

steps.title: רב נחמן asks what really happened
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רב ענן to tell him the actual incident behind שמואל's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Tell me now, how did the actual incident go?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן suspects שמואל was misunderstood, so he asks for the real story. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of rejecting שמואל, רב נחמן assumes רב ענן may have drawn the wrong rule from a specific case. Knowing the facts will show what שמואל really allowed.

phrases.english: He said to him: Tell me now,
how did the actual incident go?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא לִי אִיזִי גּוּפָא דְעוֹבָדָא הֵיכִי הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the objection by asking for the real facts behind the ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The actual case from which רב ענן learned שמואל's ruling.

steps.title: The story of the orphans' kettle
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rented out the kettle of מר עוקבא's orphans and charged both rent and payment for loss of weight.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There was a kettle of the children of מר עוקבא at שמואל's house. He would weigh it and give it out, weigh it and take it back. He took rent and also payment for the loss. Normally, if you take rent you don't take for loss, and if you take for loss you don't take rent.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ענן tells the story: שמואל charged renters of the orphans' kettle both rent and payment for the metal that wore away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually charging both is a problem: paying for loss treats the kettle like a loan, so extra rent looks like רבית. רב ענן understood that שמואל allowed this only because the owners were orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: A sage whose young children were orphans

phrases.english: He said to him: There was a certain kettle
of the children of Mar Ukva
that was in the house of Mar Shmuel.
He would weigh it and give it out,
and weigh it and take it back.
He took rent and took payment for the loss.
If rent, then not payment for loss,
and if payment for loss, then not rent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב נחמן's question by telling the incident.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שמואל charged both rent and depreciation on the orphans' kettle, which normally is not allowed.

steps.title: רב נחמן: this case is allowed even for adults
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן shows that charging both is fine here for anyone, so there is no proof for orphans.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: In a case like this, even for bearded adults it is allowed, because the owners accept the wear of the copper, since the more the copper burns, the less it is worth.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rejects the proof: what שמואל did is allowed for adults too, so it says nothing special about orphans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The kettle is a rented object that stays the owners' property, and they carry the risk. The payment for loss is just for the metal visibly burned away by use, like part of the rent. So this is not רבית at all, and nobody may lend orphans' money with real רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: Loss of the copper through wear

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's kettle case was not a special leniency for orphans. Renting an item and charging for visible wear is allowed for everyone, so it gives no license to lend orphans' money with רבית.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't conclude that orphans may take רבית. רב נחמן shows שמואל's case was not רבית in the first place.

phrases.english: He said to him: In a case like this,
even for bearded ones also
it is permitted to do so,
since they take upon themselves
the wearing away of the copper,
as the more the copper is burned,
the less its value.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא אֲפִילּוּ בְּדִקְנָנֵי נָמֵי שְׁרֵי לְמִיעְבַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב ענן's reading of the incident in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that orphans' money may be lent with רבית.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The kettle arrangement is a permitted rental for anyone, since the owners bear the wear, so it is not רבית at all.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Orphans' money may not be lent with real רבית; שמואל's case was a permitted rental.

steps.title: Orphans' money may be invested on profit-leaning terms
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, or some say רב ששת, rules that orphans' money may be lent in a deal that is close to profit and far from loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר שילא said in the name of רב חסדא (and some say רבה בר יוסף בר חמא said in the name of רב ששת): It is permitted to lend orphans' money on terms that are close to profit and far from loss.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the proof from שמואל, the גמרא brings a new and smaller leniency for orphans' money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Full רבית for orphans was rejected in Step 8. This ruling allows only a deal that leans toward profit, which is a milder problem than real רבית. For orphans, that milder problem is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say it this way. It gives a second version of who said the ruling.
Close to profit and far from loss. The deal is set up so the investor is more likely to gain than to lose.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר שֵׁילָא אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא,
phrases.english: Rabba bar Sheila said that Rav Chisda said,
and some say it this way:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Yosef bar Chama said that Rav Sheshet said:
It is permitted to lend out orphans' money
close to profit and far from loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר שֵׁילָא אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof for full רבית was rejected, this offers a narrower leniency for orphans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Orphans' money may be invested on terms that are close to profit and far from loss.

steps.title: A ברייתא grades three kinds of investment deals
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says a profit-leaning deal makes one a רשע, a loss-leaning deal makes one a חסיד, and an even deal is the normal standard.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Close to profit and far from loss is a wicked person. Close to loss and far from profit is a pious person. Close to both, or far from both, is the normal way for every person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains the phrase used in Step 9 and shows how other people are judged for such deals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For an ordinary person, a deal that leans toward profit is wrong, because it looks like רבית. This shows how special the leniency for orphans in Step 9 is. A fair deal, where the risk is even, is the normal and proper level.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. This opens a ברייתא.
A pious person who goes beyond what the law requires
The normal standard for every person

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this ברייתא contradicts Step 9. The ברייתא describes ordinary people. Step 9 is a special exception made for orphans.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Close to profit and far from loss: a wicked person.
Close to loss and far from profit: a pious person.
Close to this and to that,
or far from this and from that:
this is the standard of every person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines and grades the type of deal that Step 9 allows for orphans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A profit-leaning deal is wicked, a loss-leaning deal is pious, and an even deal is the normal standard.

steps.title: רבה asks how to manage orphans' money
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks רב יוסף what a בית דין actually does with money belonging to orphans.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to רב יוסף: This money of orphans, what do we do with it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה asks a practical question about handling orphans' money. This opens a new discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 9 and 10 dealt with what is permitted. Now the question is practical: how should the money be managed so the orphans' inheritance is kept safe?

keyTerms.meaning: How do we act? What do we do?

phrases.english: Rabba said to Rav Yosef:
This money of orphans,
what do we do with it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the permission to invest to the practical question of how to manage the money.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The proper practical way to manage orphans' funds.

steps.title: רב יוסף: a בית דין holds it and gives it out bit by bit
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that we set up a בית דין to hold the money and give it to the orphans one coin at a time.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We set up a court for them, and we give it to them coin by coin.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers that the money is kept safe by a בית דין and handed out slowly as the orphans need it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This plan keeps the money from being wasted. It does not grow the money at all, though, and Step 13 will attack exactly that point.

keyTerms.meaning: Coin by coin, a little at a time

phrases.english: He said to him:
We set up a court for them
and we give it to them coin by coin.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court holds the money and gives it out to the orphans little by little.

steps.title: רבה objects: the money will run out
steps.stepSummary: רבה argues that giving the money out without investing it will use up the principal.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But the principal is being used up!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה challenges רב יוסף's plan, because the orphans' money would just shrink until nothing is left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Keeping the money safe is not enough. If it never earns anything, spending it slowly still uses it all up. Good guardians should keep the estate going.

keyTerms.meaning: But look! This word opens a challenge.
The principal (the main sum) is used up

phrases.english: He said to him:
But the principal is being used up!

steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's method of handing out the money coin by coin
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Money that is never invested gets used up, so the orphans' estate will be gone.

steps.title: רב יוסף asks רבה for his own method
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף asks רבה what he does instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What does the Master do?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף turns the question back to רבה and asks for his better method. This sets up רבה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף does not defend his own plan. Instead he asks רבה to offer a method that both protects the money and lets it grow.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master. A respectful way of saying 'you.'

phrases.english: He said to him:
The Master, what does he do?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the objection by asking רבה for his method.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבה's own practical method for managing orphans' money.

steps.title: רבה: buy scrap gold and invest it back with the seller
steps.stepSummary: רבה finds a man with scrap gold, buys it with the orphans' money, and gives it back to him as an investment on profit-leaning terms.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We look for a man who has scrap gold, we take gold from him, and we give it to him on terms close to profit and far from loss.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה explains his method, which uses the leniency from Step 9 so that the orphans' money grows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The orphans now own real gold, so their money is backed by something solid. That gold is then invested with the same man on terms that favor the orphans, exactly as Step 9 allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Scrap gold, broken pieces of gold

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the leniency of Step 9 being used in real life to protect and grow orphans' estates.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: בָּדְקִינַן גַּבְרָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ דַּהֲבָא פְּרִיכָא,
phrases.english: We look for a man who has scrap gold,
and we take the gold from him,
phrases.notes: He means we buy the gold from him with the orphans' money.

phrases.english: and we give it to him
close to profit and far from loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּדְקִינַן גַּבְרָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ דַּהֲבָא פְּרִיכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's question with רבה's method.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Buy scrap gold and invest it with the seller on terms close to profit and far from loss.

steps.title: Not a recognizable item, because it may belong to someone else
steps.stepSummary: Only scrap gold is bought, not a distinct item, because a distinct item might be a deposit that its true owner could identify and take back.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a distinct item, no. Perhaps it is a deposit, and its owner will come, give identifying signs, and take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבה said scrap gold in particular. A recognizable object is avoided.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A finished object has features that can be recognized. If the seller was only holding it for someone else, the real owner could prove it is his with סימנים and take it, and the orphans would lose. Scrap gold has no such signs, so it is safe.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit, something left with a person for safekeeping

steps.whatToRemember: In רבה's method, the gold bought for the orphans must be scrap gold, not a recognizable item, because a recognizable item might be someone else's deposit that could be claimed back with סימנים.

phrases.english: But a distinct item, no,
perhaps they are a deposit,
and its owner will come and give identifying signs
and take it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and limits רבה's method to scrap gold only.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not buy a recognizable item for orphans, because it may be a deposit that its owner could reclaim with identifying signs.

steps.title: What if no one has scrap gold?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי challenges רבה's method: if no man with scrap gold can be found, the orphans' money will be used up.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: That works if we find a man who has scrap gold. But if we can't find such a man, should the orphans' money just get eaten away?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי attacks רבה's solution as too limited, since it depends on finding a man with scrap gold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's method is safe but narrow, because it needs one specific kind of person. If that person can't be found, we are back to רבה's own complaint in step 13: the money gets spent with no profit. רב אשי wants a method that always works.

keyTerms.meaning: That works out well (for one case, but not another)
Scrap gold, broken pieces of gold

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It works out well if a man is found
who has scrap gold,
phrases.notes: This is the method רבה described in step 15.

phrases.english: but if no man is found
who has scrap gold,
shall the orphans' money be used up?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how practical רבה's scrap-gold method (steps 15-16) really is.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's method of investing through a man with scrap gold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The method depends on a person who may not be available. When he isn't, the orphans' money is spent down, which is the very problem רבה raised.

steps.title: רב אשי's method: a trustworthy, law-abiding man with secure property
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says to find a man whose property is undisputed, who is trustworthy and obeys Torah law without needing to be forced, and give him the money in front of a בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: We look for a man whose property is free of disputes, who is trustworthy, who obeys Torah law and never needs to be put in שמתא by the Rabbis, and we give him the money in front of a בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי replaces the scrap-gold method with a more practical one that can always be used: pick a reliable person and hand him the money through a בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each condition protects the orphans. Undisputed property means there is something safe to collect from. Being trustworthy and obeying the court willingly means he will pay without a fight. Giving the money in front of a בית דין makes the deal official and on record.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose property is quiet, meaning no one disputes his ownership
Excommunication, a ban the בית דין puts on someone who disobeys

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי's final method: the orphans' money is invested with a man who has secure property, is trustworthy, and obeys the court willingly, and the handover is done in front of a בית דין.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
We look for a man whose property is quiet,
phrases.notes: "Quiet" means no one has a claim against his property. It is clearly his.

phrases.english: and who is trustworthy,
and who listens to the law of the Torah
and does not receive excommunication from the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: He means a person who obeys the court on his own, so he never has to be put under a ban.

phrases.english: and we give it to him in court.
phrases.notes: The money is given on the same profit-leaning business terms described in step 15.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's own challenge in step 17 by offering a method that does not depend on scrap gold.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the earlier method with a broader, always-available procedure
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only safe way to invest orphans' money is through a man with scrap gold, as רבה said.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any man with undisputed property who is trustworthy and obeys the court willingly may receive the money in front of a בית דין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical standard for how a בית דין protects and grows money that belongs to orphans.
